seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.note: According to dates and times stamped on this telegram, it was sent by JJ from Trieste on 31 May 1920 at “12.50” (p.m.), and was received in Sirmione on 1 June at “8.39” (a.m.).

“departure held up due to strike will write.” JJ did write a long letter, most likely also on 31 May 1920, to explain that he had been prevented from leaving Trieste by the wreck of a passenger train on the line and by cancellations resulting from a railway strike. Now he hoped, he said, to meet Pound in England, en route for Ireland, sometime in the near future, as his present plan was to get out of Trieste for several months and finish Ulysses in Dublin or Galway in the relative peace of his nuclear family (Pound/Joyce 167-69; LII 467-69). Richard Ellmann dates JJ’s letter 5 June 1920 (LII 467; SL 252), but Forrest Read more cogently makes it 31 May for reasons internal and external to the epistolary documents (Pound/Joyce 167). Despite JJ’s trouble getting to Sirmione, he did manage to arrive there, with his son Giorgio, on the night of 8 June 1920, and spent two days with Pound and his wife Dorothy. For a more complete account of JJ’s visit to Sirmione, see JJ telegram to Pound, 26 May 1920, notes.

note.p: The reverse of the message side of this telegram contains arithmetic calculations in what appears to be Pound’s hand. It is difficult to know exactly what they mean, but it is quite possible that they represent attempts to determine whether and how much Pound could contribute to a visit to Sirmione by JJ and his family. Pound’s letters to JJ between 2 and 8 June 1920 are filled with ideas to tempt JJ to the Lake Garda paradise, including an offer of a gift of 1,000 lire to tide JJ over, and affordable rooms at Albergo de la Pace for JJ and three family members at 14 lire a day for one person or 56 lire for four, meals included, “& view on lake & with garden” (Pound/Joyce 170-73). Pound’s letter to JJ of 7-8 June 1920 shows that he was also reckoning how much JJ was making by teaching in Trieste—another possible reason for some of the numbers scratched on this telegram (Pound/Joyce 176-77).

Pound’s generous desire to provide financial assistance, characteristic in any case, was probably fortified by his having received, around 1 June 1920, “2050 lire. (alias $100)” from the New York magazine The Dial, for which he was now acting as a paid foreign agent and correspondent. The New York lawyer and art patron John Quinn (1870-1924), who had helped to subsidize The Little Review when Pound served as its foreign editor, had also helped arrange Pound’s new role with The Dial, for which Pound was grateful (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 187).

It is worth noting that Pound was also at this time calculating the number of pounds it might take to get his friend, the American poet and critic T.S. Eliot (1888-1965), out of his time-consuming job in Lloyds Bank in London. Eliot wrote him circa June 1920 with an account of his annual earnings and expectations (The Letters of T.S. Eliot, vol. 1, ed. Valerie Eliot [New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1988], 385). The effort culminated in Pound’s impetuous scheme, Bel Esprit, to get thirty people to subscribe £10 a year to liberate Eliot from the bank. When the idea began to get about, Eliot panicked at the publicity, and Bel Esprit faded out by late 1922 (Humphrey Carpenter, A Serious Character: The Life of Ezra Pound [Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1988], 409-412).
